```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
target <- params$target
config.file.label <- params$biomarker_file
target.dir <- params$target_dir
table.dir <- file.path(target.dir, "tables")
figure.dir <- file.path(target.dir, "figures")
read_report_table <- function(name) {
  read.csv(file.path(table.dir, name), check.names = FALSE)
}
format_report_number <- function(x, digits = 3) {
  formatC(x, digits = digits, format = "fg")
}
format_report_p_value <- function(x) {
  ifelse(
    is.na(x),
    "not estimable",
    ifelse(x < 0.001, format(x, scientific = TRUE, digits = 2), sprintf("%.3f", x))
  )
}
dependency <- read_report_table("04_dependency_summary.csv")
modality.coverage <- read_report_table("01_modality_coverage.csv")
lineage.global <- read_report_table("05_lineage_global_test.csv")
lineages <- read_report_table("06_lineage_associations.csv")
target.associations <- read_report_table("07_target_associations.csv")
expression <- read_report_table("08_top_expression_associations.csv")
mutations <- read_report_table("09_top_mutation_associations.csv")
copy.number <- read_report_table("10_top_copy_number_associations.csv")
expression.all <- readRDS(file.path(target.dir, "intermediate", "expression_associations.rds"))
mutation.all <- readRDS(file.path(target.dir, "intermediate", "mutation_associations.rds"))
copy.number.all <- readRDS(file.path(target.dir, "intermediate", "copy_number_associations.rds"))
special.features <- readRDS(file.path(target.dir, "intermediate", "special_features.rds"))
lineage.specific <- read_report_table("11_lineage_specific_associations.csv")
feature.designation <- read_report_table("12_feature_designation.csv")
model.coefficients <- read_report_table("13_integrated_model_coefficients.csv")
selection.stability <- read_report_table("14_selection_stability.csv")
model.performance <- read_report_table("15_nested_cv_performance.csv")
model.predictions <- read_report_table("16_nested_cv_predictions.csv")
if (!"pearson_r" %in% names(model.performance)) {
  model.performance$pearson_r <- vapply(
    model.performance$repeat_id,
    function(repeat.id) {
      repeat.rows <- model.predictions$repeat_id == repeat.id
      cor(
        model.predictions$observed[repeat.rows],
        model.predictions$predicted[repeat.rows],
        use = "complete.obs", method = "pearson"
      )
    },
    numeric(1)
  )
}
lineage.performance <- read_report_table("17_lineage_cv_performance.csv")
quality.checks <- read_report_table("02_data_quality_checks.csv")
```

This pipeline integrates CRISPR dependency with lineage, expression, copy number and damaging somatic mutations from **`r params$release`**. Please note, throughout the report, more negative Chronos scores indicate that knocking out the target gene has a stronger effect on cell fitness. This is interpreted as stronger dependency on the target gene selected, in this case: **`r target`**.

This report addresses the following question:

**Which molecular features are associated with dependency on `r target`, and which exploratory molecular predictors are reproducible in held-out cancer cell line models?**

In other words, the report first describes individual associations and then asks which eligible molecular features remain useful when every modality is considered jointly while allowing lineage to have different baseline dependency levels. The integrated model estimates one common molecular effect; it does not test whether that effect changes between lineages.

The overall report narrative is structured as follows:

- Eligibility and data quality
- Dependency distribution and cancer-lineage characterisation
- Self-associations between the dependency of `r target` and its own expression, damaging mutation and copy number
- Associations between the dependency of `r target` and pre-specified hypotheses, followed by within-lineage follow-up
- Associations between the dependency of `r target` and genome-wide expression, damaging mutation and copy number
- Integrated exploratory modelling
- Nested cross-validation performance

# How to read this report

The purpose of this report is to explain why cancer cell line models differ in their dependency on **`r target`**, going from simple descriptions to an integrated analysis.
First, it asks whether each measurement is reliable enough to analyse. It then shows what each feature does by itself, before allowing every eligible molecular feature to compete under the same regularization while accounting for lineage-specific baseline dependency. This additive adjustment does not represent molecular effects that vary between lineages; those require a feature-by-lineage interaction analysis.
The final results are a prioritisation of reproducible exploratory predictors.

The analysis has four layers:

### 1. Eligibility: can the feature be analysed reliably?

Eligibility is a data quality decision made before interpreting an association. Features are excluded when the available data cannot support the planned comparison. This is the first layer of data filtering and applies in all analyses.

| Feature type | Eligibility rule | Biological/statistical reason |
|---|---|---|
| Expression | Observed in at least 80% of models with any expression-assay data and has nonzero variance | A feature needs sufficient coverage and variation within the assayed models to compare them meaningfully. |
| Copy number | Observed in at least 80% of models with any copy-number-assay data and has nonzero variance | Sparse or constant measurements within the assayed models cannot support a reliable correlation. |
| Damaging mutation | At least 3 altered and 3 wild type models | Both biological groups must be represented well enough for an altered-versus-wild type comparison. |

As per the data, there are three types of features described below. These modality rules apply equally to all three roles:

- **Target-characterisation features:** `r target` expression, damaging mutation and copy number.
- **Pre-specified hypotheses:** features supplied in `r if (nzchar(config.file.label)) config.file.label else "an optional biomarker YAML file"` are nominated before modelling from existing biological knowledge. YAML designation does not override insufficient coverage, zero variance or the mutation 10/10 rule.
- **Genome-wide candidates:** every other expression, mutation and copy number feature that passes the same basic modality-specific eligibility rule enters the integrated molecular search.

### 2. Univariate association: what does each feature show by itself?

The univariate screen asks: **is this feature associated with `r target` dependency when considered on its own?** For example, it tests whether `r target` Chronos scores increases or decreases with Gene X expression, or whether models carrying a damaging Gene X mutation have different `r target` dependency scores from Gene X wild type models.

- Expression uses a Spearman correlation, making it less sensitive to extreme values and distributional assumptions. Negative correlation indicates stronger dependency as expression increases.
- Damaging mutations use R's built-in unequal-variance Welch t-test to compare mean dependency in altered and wild type models. The mean difference, 95% confidence interval and P value come from the same test.
- Copy number uses Pearson correlation, which is appropriate for continuous measurements that are approximately normally distributed.

FDR is calculated per modality. An expression result is considered notable when FDR < 0.05 and |Spearman rho| >= 0.30; a copy number result requires FDR < 0.05 and |Pearson r| >= 0.30; a mutation result requires FDR < 0.05. These thresholds identify significant associations only.

### 3. Predictor designation: how is each eligible feature treated?

After eligibility is established, the integrated model treats every eligible molecular feature equally, without privileging a particular modality or pre-specified hypothesis. The model uses elastic-net regularization to select a subset of features that reproducibly predict `r target` dependency in held-out cell line models.

- **Target characterisation:** eligible `r target` expression, damaging mutation and copy number describe the molecular state of the target.
- **Pre-specified hypothesis:** eligible YAML features represent hypotheses nominated before modelling from biological knowledge.
- **Genome-wide candidate:** every other eligible expression, mutation and copy-number feature.
- **Lineage adjustment:** cancer-lineage indicators account for broad histological differences in baseline dependency. In the integrated model they prevent a molecular coefficient from being driven solely by different lineage composition, but they do not allow the molecular coefficient itself to vary by lineage.

Every eligible molecular feature enters with penalty factor 1 and can be reduced to zero. Only lineage indicators receive penalty factor 0.

### 4. Integrated exploratory model: what remains useful when the data are considered together?

The integrated model asks: **after accounting for different lineage baselines, which eligible molecular features contribute reproducibly to prediction of `r target` dependency when all molecular measurements compete under the same regularization?** It estimates a common molecular effect across lineages. It does not test whether a feature has a stronger, weaker or opposite effect in a particular lineage.

The parameter choices are:

- **Gaussian model:** Chronos dependency is a continuous numerical measurement, so the model predicts a number rather than a category.
- **Elastic net balance (`alpha = 0.5`):** this is a middle ground balance between selecting a small set of features and retaining groups of correlated biological features that may be correlated and carry similar information.
- **One SD lambda:** several model sizes may predict almost equally well. This rule chooses the simpler, more strongly regularized model when its estimated error is still statistically comparable to the best performing model.
- **Nested cross-validation:** the same training portion is used for feature selection and parameter choice, and the outer held-out portion is used to estimate performance. This avoids overfitting and data leakage.
- **Repeated folds:** repeating the five-fold analysis three times reduces dependence on one arbitrary division of the dataset.

<details class="model-construction-details">
<summary><strong>Read more details on the model construction</strong></summary>

<div class="model-details-box">

In concrete terms, each repeat divides the cell line models into five lineage-balanced outer folds, which can be called A–E. The model is trained on A–D and tested on E, then trained on A–C plus E and tested on D, continuing until each fold has served as the test set once. Within every four-fold training portion, a separate five-fold inner cross-validation chooses the one-standard-error lambda; the outer test fold is not used for preprocessing, feature selection or parameter choice. The full A–E assignment is then reshuffled, while preserving lineage balance, and the process is repeated twice more. Thus, the procedure produces 15 outer fitted models and three complete sets of held-out predictions, one set per repeat.

The results are collated in three ways:

- **Held-out performance:** within each repeat, the five outer test-fold predictions are joined so every cell model has one held-out prediction. Pearson r, RMSE and R² are calculated for that complete prediction set. The report then summarizes their variation across the three repeats.
- **Molecular feature stability:** for each molecular feature, selection is counted across all 15 outer models. Selection frequency is the number of nonzero coefficients divided by 15. Direction concordance is the proportion of the feature's nonzero coefficients that agree with its most common direction.
- **Full-data fit and reported stable set:** the same model specification is fitted once more using all eligible cell line models, with inner cross-validation choosing `lambda.1se`. A molecular feature is reported as stable only when its outer-model selection frequency is at least 60%, its direction concordance is at least 80%, and its coefficient is also nonzero in this full-data fit. The displayed coefficient comes from that fit, and the stable set is a reporting filter, not a second refitted model.

<div class="stability-callout">

A molecular feature is called stable only if it is selected in at least 60% of outer models, has the same coefficient direction in at least 80% of models in which it is selected, and remains nonzero in the full-data fit.

The report therefore presents selection frequency, direction concordance and nested-CV Pearson r, RMSE and R². Stable genes are exploratory molecular predictors associated with `r target` dependency ready to follow-up in future experiments.

</div>

</div>

</details>

# Dependency distribution

The first exploratory question is whether dependency on `r target` is observed in a subset of DepMap pancancer cell line models or is a broadly distributed dependency. The distribution of Chronos scores across all models is shown below:

```{r distribution-figure, out.width='90%', fig.align='center'}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figure.dir, "01_dependency_distribution.png"))
```

Across `r dependency$n` models, the median `r target` Chronos score was `r format_report_number(dependency$median)`. The proportion of cell lines with Chronos scores below -0.5 (what is generally considered as *strong dependency*) was `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * dependency$proportion_below_minus_0_5)`.

---

# Lineage specificity

Cancer types can differ in which genes they require for survival. Before examining individual molecular features, the question is whether `r target` dependency is concentrated in particular cancer lineages.
The plot below shows the size and direction of these differences, while the global Kruskal–Wallis test evaluates if there is evidence of an overall lineage association.

```{r lineage-global-interpretation, results='asis'}
if (is.na(lineage.global$p_value)) {
  cat("The global lineage comparison could not be estimated for this target.\n")
} else if (lineage.global$p_value < 0.05) {
  cat(sprintf(
    "The global comparison found evidence that **%s dependency differs across cancer lineages** (Kruskal–Wallis P = %s). This means that at least one lineage has a different dependency distribution; the comparisons below show which lineages may contribute to the pattern.\n",
    target,
    format_report_p_value(lineage.global$p_value)
  ))
} else {
  cat(sprintf(
    "The global comparison found **no clear evidence that %s dependency differs across cancer lineages** (Kruskal–Wallis P = %s). On the basis of this overall test, no lineage should be considered a 'distinct dependency context'.\n",
    target,
    format_report_p_value(lineage.global$p_value)
  ))
}
```

```{r lineage-figure, out.width='95%', fig.align='center'}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figure.dir, "02_lineage_dependency.png"))
```

To identify which lineages may contribute to this variation, each lineage was compared with all other eligible lineages combined. The table reports the leading lineage-versus-rest results. Negative **median differences** indicate stronger dependency in that lineage, whereas positive differences indicate weaker dependency.

```{r lineage-table}
knitr::kable(head(lineages[order(lineages$fdr), ], 10), digits = 3, caption = "Leading lineage associations")
```

```{r lineage-interpretation, results='asis'}
significant.lineages <- lineages[!is.na(lineages$fdr) & lineages$fdr < 0.05, ]

if (is.na(lineage.global$p_value) || lineage.global$p_value >= 0.05) {
  cat(sprintf(
    "There was no clear evidence that **%s dependency varies by lineage**. No particular lineage should be treated as a lineage-specific dependency context.\n",
    target
  ))
} else if (!nrow(significant.lineages)) {
  cat(sprintf(
    "The global test suggests that **%s dependency varies across lineages**, but no individual lineage-versus-rest comparison remained significant after FDR correction. The data supports overall lineage variation without identifying a specific contributing lineage.\n",
    target
  ))
} else {
  stronger.lineages <- significant.lineages[
    significant.lineages$median_difference < 0,
  ]
  weaker.lineages <- significant.lineages[
    significant.lineages$median_difference > 0,
  ]

  if (nrow(stronger.lineages)) {
    stronger.lineages <- stronger.lineages[
      order(stronger.lineages$fdr, stronger.lineages$median_difference),
    ]
    stronger.examples <- head(stronger.lineages, 2L)
    stronger.text <- paste(
      sprintf(
        "**%s** (median difference %s; FDR %s)",
        stronger.examples$lineage,
        format_report_number(stronger.examples$median_difference),
        format_report_p_value(stronger.examples$fdr)
      ),
      collapse = " and "
    )
    cat(sprintf(
      "%s contributed to the lineage association through more-negative dependency scores than the remaining models, indicating **stronger %s dependency** in those cancer contexts. ",
      stronger.text,
      target
    ))
  }

  if (nrow(weaker.lineages)) {
    weaker.lineages <- weaker.lineages[
      order(weaker.lineages$fdr, -weaker.lineages$median_difference),
    ]
    weaker.examples <- head(weaker.lineages, 2L)
    weaker.text <- paste(
      sprintf(
        "**%s** (median difference +%s; FDR %s)",
        weaker.examples$lineage,
        format_report_number(weaker.examples$median_difference),
        format_report_p_value(weaker.examples$fdr)
      ),
      collapse = " and "
    )
    cat(sprintf(
      "%s contributed through more-positive scores, indicating **weaker %s dependency** relative to the remaining models. ",
      weaker.text,
      target
    ))
  }

  cat("\nThese results show that lineage captures systematic differences in dependency and could confound molecular associations.\n")
}
```

<div class="stability-callout">

Interpretation note: Lineage associations may reflect molecular features enriched in particular histologies. For example, an apparent association between Gene X mutation and `r target` dependency could partly arise because the mutation is common in a lineage already more dependent on `r target`. The integrated model therefore forces lineage indicators into every fit to reduce this potential confounding.

</div>

# Target characterisation

Next, the selected target `r target`'s expression, damaging mutation status and copy number were evaluated for association with `r target` dependency. The table below shows the corresponding statistical results.

The plot below shows the correlation between dependency and the target's own expression.

```{r target-association-table}
target.associations.display <- target.associations[, c(
  "feature", "test", "n", "estimate_type", "estimate",
  "p_value", "fdr", "eligible"
)]
names(target.associations.display) <- c(
  "Feature", "Test", "N", "Estimate type", "Estimate",
  "P value", "FDR", "Eligible"
)
knitr::kable(
  target.associations.display,
  digits = 3,
  caption = paste(target, "molecular-state associations with dependency")
)
```

For the expression and copy number rows, a negative correlation indicates stronger dependency as the measurement increases. For the mutation row, a negative estimate indicates stronger dependency in models carrying a damaging mutation. These are unadjusted associations and may reflect lineage or other correlated molecular features.

```{r expression-figure, out.width='90%', fig.align='center'}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figure.dir, "03_expression_dependency.png"))
```

<details>
<summary><strong>Interpretations</strong></summary>
<br>
**Expression**

A negative expression–dependency correlation can indicate that cells hyperexpressing `r target` are more reliant on it (sometimes called an expression-linked dependency or “addiction”). This may suggest that the active pathway or cellular state marked by high expression requires that gene.

A positive correlation means highly expressing cells are less sensitive to knockout. This could reflect compensatory expression, association with a resistant lineage, or stronger dependency among low-expression cells.

**Damaging mutations**

If $\Delta$ (altered - wild type) < 0, cells carrying a damaging mutation are more dependent on that gene. This may indicate that the mutation is activating, dominant negative, or otherwise sensitising.

If $\Delta$ (altered - wild type) > 0, mutated cells are less dependent on the target. This may indicate pathway redundancy, target-pathway inactivation, or resistance.

For a gene’s mutation versus its own dependency, a positive difference is often biologically plausible: if the gene is already functionally inactivated, CRISPR knockout may have little additional effect.

**Copy number**

A negative correlation means higher copy number is associated with stronger target dependency. For the target’s own copy number, this can suggest an amplification-associated dependency: amplified cells may become reliant on the overactive or overexpressed target.

A positive correlation means higher copy number is associated with weaker dependency, or equivalently, lower copy number cells are more dependent. This might reflect vulnerability after partial deletion, dosage-sensitive biology, lineage differences, or genomic features linked to the copy number event.

</details>

# Pre-specified hypotheses

`r if (nzchar(config.file.label)) paste0("Features listed in **", config.file.label, "** are") else "Features supplied through an optional biomarker YAML file are"` pre-specified hypotheses nominated before modelling from existing biological knowledge. Their designation makes their results easy to follow but does not force them into the fitted result or change their penalty. Each eligible hypothesis competes on equal terms with every other molecular feature (see [3. Predictor designation: how is each eligible feature treated?](#predictor-designation-how-is-each-eligible-feature-treated)). Their pan-cancer results are shown below under each nominated gene.

```{r prespecified-association-data, include=FALSE}
empty.special.associations <- data.frame(
  Gene = character(),
  Feature = character(),
  Modality = character(),
  Test = character(),
  N = character(),
  `Estimate type` = character(),
  Estimate = numeric(),
  `P value` = numeric(),
  FDR = numeric(),
  Eligible = logical(),
  check.names = FALSE
)
make.special.associations <- function(modality, genes) {
  if (!length(genes)) return(empty.special.associations)
  if (modality == "expression") {
    rows <- expression.all[match(genes, expression.all$gene), ]
    return(data.frame(
      Gene = genes,
      Feature = paste(genes, "expression"),
      Modality = "Expression",
      Test = "Spearman correlation",
      N = as.character(rows$n),
      `Estimate type` = "Spearman rho",
      Estimate = rows$spearman_rho,
      `P value` = rows$p_value,
      FDR = rows$fdr,
      Eligible = rows$eligible,
      check.names = FALSE
    ))
  }
  if (modality == "mutation") {
    rows <- mutation.all[match(genes, mutation.all$gene), ]
    return(data.frame(
      Gene = genes,
      Feature = paste(genes, "damaging mutation"),
      Modality = "Mutation",
      Test = "Welch mean comparison",
      N = sprintf("%s altered / %s wild type", rows$altered_n, rows$reference_n),
      `Estimate type` = "Altered minus wild type",
      Estimate = rows$effect,
      `P value` = rows$p_value,
      FDR = rows$fdr,
      Eligible = rows$eligible,
      check.names = FALSE
    ))
  }
  rows <- copy.number.all[match(genes, copy.number.all$gene), ]
  data.frame(
    Gene = genes,
    Feature = paste(genes, "copy number"),
    Modality = "Copy number",
    Test = "Pearson correlation",
    N = as.character(rows$n),
    `Estimate type` = "Pearson r",
    Estimate = rows$correlation,
    `P value` = rows$p_value,
    FDR = rows$fdr,
    Eligible = rows$eligible,
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}
prespecified.associations <- rbind(
  make.special.associations(
    "expression", special.features$configured$expression
  ),
  make.special.associations(
    "mutation", special.features$configured$mutation
  ),
  make.special.associations(
    "copy_number", special.features$configured$copy_number
  )
)
```

```{r prespecified-association-table, results='asis'}
if (nrow(prespecified.associations)) {
  for (hypothesis.gene in unique(prespecified.associations$Gene)) {
    hypothesis.rows <- prespecified.associations[
      prespecified.associations$Gene == hypothesis.gene,
      setdiff(names(prespecified.associations), "Gene"),
      drop = FALSE
    ]
    cat(sprintf("\n## %s\n\n", hypothesis.gene))
    print(knitr::kable(
      hypothesis.rows,
      digits = 3,
      caption = paste(hypothesis.gene, "molecular-state associations with", target, "dependency")
    ))
    cat("\n")
  }
} else {
  cat("NB: No pre-specified hypotheses were supplied for this analysis.\n")
}
```

# Lineage-specific molecular associations

An additional layer of the analysis computes associations between `r target` dependency and its target-characterisation features, and between `r target` dependency and the pre-specified hypotheses, separately within each cancer lineage. This shows whether an association is present within a lineage and whether a pancancer association may be explained by lineage composition. These separate estimates are descriptive: they do not formally test whether the feature effect differs between lineages. A formal comparison requires a feature-by-lineage interaction model.

The combined table below retains both estimable and non-estimable target/pre-specified-hypothesis rows (sorted by FDR). When a lineage lacks enough models, variation or mutation group stratification, the *Reason* column explains why no estimate or FDR is available.

<details>
<summary><strong>Target and pre-specified-hypothesis associations within lineages, ordered by FDR</strong></summary>
<br>

```{r lineage-specific-table}
lineage.specific.display <- lineage.specific[, c(
  "family", "feature", "modality", "lineage", "n", "altered_n",
  "reference_n", "estimate_type", "estimate", "fdr", "conf_low",
  "conf_high", "p_value", "estimable", "reason"
)]
lineage.specific.display$family <- c(
  target_characterization = "Target characterisation",
  prespecified_hypothesis = "Pre-specified hypothesis"
)[lineage.specific.display$family]
lineage.specific.display$modality <- c(
  expression = "Expression",
  mutation = "Damaging mutation",
  copy_number = "Copy number"
)[lineage.specific.display$modality]
names(lineage.specific.display) <- c(
  "Source", "Feature", "Modality", "Lineage", "N", "Altered N",
  "Wild type N", "Estimate type", "Estimate", "FDR", "95% CI low",
  "95% CI high", "P value", "Estimable", "Reason"
)
lineage.specific.display <- lineage.specific.display[
  order(
    is.na(lineage.specific.display$FDR),
    lineage.specific.display$FDR,
    lineage.specific.display$`P value`,
    lineage.specific.display$Feature,
    lineage.specific.display$Lineage
  ),
]
# DataTables otherwise treats blank FDR values inconsistently during client-side
# sorting. Use an invisible value above the valid FDR range so blanks sort last.
lineage.specific.display$`FDR sort` <- ifelse(
  is.na(lineage.specific.display$FDR),
  2,
  lineage.specific.display$FDR
)
lineage.specific.display$FDR <- ifelse(
  is.na(lineage.specific.display$FDR),
  "NA",
  formatC(lineage.specific.display$FDR, format = "f", digits = 3)
)
lineage.specific.widget <- DT::datatable(
  lineage.specific.display,
  rownames = FALSE,
  options = list(
    pageLength = 10,
    lengthMenu = c(10, 25, 50),
    searching = FALSE,
    scrollX = TRUE,
    autoWidth = TRUE,
    order = list(list(9, "asc")),
    columnDefs = list(
      list(targets = 15, visible = FALSE, searchable = FALSE),
      list(targets = 9, orderData = 15)
    )
  )
)
DT::formatRound(
  lineage.specific.widget,
  columns = c("Estimate", "95% CI low", "95% CI high", "P value"),
  digits = 3
)
```

</details>

```{r lineage-specific-highlights, results='asis'}
significant.feature.lineages <- lineage.specific[
  lineage.specific$estimable &
    !is.na(lineage.specific$fdr) &
    lineage.specific$fdr < 0.05,
]
if (nrow(significant.feature.lineages)) {
  cat("\n**The following association(s) passed the 5% lineage-specific FDR threshold:**\n\n")
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(significant.feature.lineages))) {
    result <- significant.feature.lineages[i, ]
    dependency.direction <- if (result$estimate < 0) "stronger" else "weaker"
    feature.contrast <- if (result$modality == "mutation") {
      "change in Chronos score in altered versus wild type models"
    } else {
      "change in Chronos score per 1 overall SD increase"
    }
    cat(sprintf(
      "- **%s was associated with %s %s dependency in %s** (estimate %s %s; 95%% CI %s to %s; FDR %s).\n",
      result$feature,
      dependency.direction,
      target,
      result$lineage,
      format_report_number(result$estimate),
      feature.contrast,
      format_report_number(result$conf_low),
      format_report_number(result$conf_high),
      format_report_p_value(result$fdr)
    ))
  }
} else {
  cat(sprintf(
    "No target self-association or pre-specified hypotheses were associated with %s dependency within a named lineage after 5%% FDR correction.\n",
    target
  ))
}
```

# Genomic associations

The following sections show the leading genes from the complete genome-wide univariate screens. The aim is to identify genome-wide molecular features flagging models with stronger or weaker `r target` dependency.

Look out for coloured points for each modality in the plots below indicating features that passed the thresholds for significance (FDR < 0.05 and |rho| >= 0.30 for expression, FDR < 0.05 for mutation, and FDR < 0.05 and |r| >= 0.30 for copy number).

### Gene expression

```{r genome-expression-figure, out.width='90%', fig.align='center'}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figure.dir, "04_expression_associations.png"))
```

```{r genome-expression-text, results='asis'}
eligible.expression <- expression.all[
  expression.all$eligible &
    is.finite(expression.all$spearman_rho),
]
notable.expression <- eligible.expression[
  !is.na(eligible.expression$fdr) &
    eligible.expression$fdr < 0.05 &
    abs(eligible.expression$spearman_rho) >= 0.30,
]

if (!nrow(notable.expression)) {
  cat(sprintf(
    "No genome-wide expression correlation was both significant at 5%% FDR and at least moderate in magnitude (|rho| >= 0.30). This screen found no substantial expression association with `%s` dependency.\n",
    target
  ))
} else {
  top.expression <- notable.expression[1, ]
  expression.strength <- top.expression$correlation_strength
  dependency.direction <- if (
    top.expression$spearman_rho < 0
  ) "stronger" else "weaker"
  cat(sprintf(
    "The leading qualifying expression association was **%s** (a %s correlation; rho %s; FDR %s), corresponding to %s `%s` dependency as expression increased.\n",
    top.expression$gene,
    expression.strength,
    format_report_number(top.expression$spearman_rho),
    format_report_p_value(top.expression$fdr),
    dependency.direction,
    target
  ))
}
```

```{r mutation-text, results='asis'}
              top.mutation$gene, format_report_number(top.mutation$effect), format_report_p_value(top.mutation$fdr), target))
} else cat(sprintf(
```

### Copy number

```{r copy-figure, out.width='90%', fig.align='center'}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figure.dir, "06_copy_number_associations.png"))
```

```{r copy-text, results='asis'}
significant.copy.number <- copy.number[!is.na(copy.number$fdr) & copy.number$fdr < 0.05, ]
if (nrow(significant.copy.number)) {
  top.copy.number <- significant.copy.number[1, ]
  cat(sprintf("The leading copy number association was **%s** (a %s correlation; r %s; FDR %s).\n",
              top.copy.number$gene, top.copy.number$correlation_strength, format_report_number(top.copy.number$correlation), format_report_p_value(top.copy.number$fdr)))
} else cat("No copy number feature passed the pre-specified 5% FDR threshold.\n")

eligible.copy.number <- copy.number.all[
  copy.number.all$eligible &
    is.finite(copy.number.all$correlation),
]
notable.copy.number <- eligible.copy.number[
  !is.na(eligible.copy.number$fdr) &
    eligible.copy.number$fdr < 0.05 &
    abs(eligible.copy.number$correlation) >= 0.30,
]

if (!nrow(notable.copy.number)) {
  cat(sprintf(
    "No genome-wide copy number correlation was both significant at 5%% FDR and at least moderate in magnitude (|r| >= 0.30). This screen found no substantial copy number association with either stronger or weaker `%s` dependency.\n",
    target
  ))
} else {
  stronger.copy.number <- notable.copy.number[notable.copy.number$correlation < 0, ]
  weaker.copy.number <- notable.copy.number[notable.copy.number$correlation > 0, ]
  direction.text <- character()

  if (nrow(stronger.copy.number)) {
    strongest.negative <- stronger.copy.number[which.min(stronger.copy.number$correlation), ]
    direction.text <- c(direction.text, sprintf(
      "**%s** showed the strongest association with greater dependency (r = %s)",
      strongest.negative$gene,
      format_report_number(strongest.negative$correlation)
    ))
  }
  if (nrow(weaker.copy.number)) {
    strongest.positive <- weaker.copy.number[which.max(weaker.copy.number$correlation), ]
    direction.text <- c(direction.text, sprintf(
      "**%s** showed the strongest association with weaker dependency (r = %s)",
      strongest.positive$gene,
      format_report_number(strongest.positive$correlation)
    ))
  }
  cat(paste0(paste(direction.text, collapse = "; "), ".\n"))
}
```

The plot above summarises the leading copy number associations. Pink points pass both the 5% FDR threshold and |Pearson r| >= 0.30; grey points fail one or both criteria. Expand the section below to inspect coverage, correlation magnitude and statistical results.

# Integrated exploratory model

This model asks which molecular features help predict `r target` dependency when the data are considered together. All eligible expression, mutation and copy number features compete under the same penalty, including the target's own features and the pre-specified hypotheses. Cancer lineage is included without a penalty to adjust for broad differences between cancer types. The molecular coefficients are common-effect estimates; lineage-specific molecular effects are not tested by this model.

The model uses Gaussian elastic net (`alpha = 0.5`) and the more conservative one-standard-error lambda. Data preparation and feature selection are repeated within the training folds so held-out models do not influence the result. A feature is called *stable* when it is selected repeatedly, keeps the same direction, and is also nonzero in the full-data fit. More construction detail and the exact thresholds are provided in the workflow explanation above (see [4. Integrated exploratory model: what remains useful when the data are considered together?](#integrated-exploratory-model-what-remains-useful-when-the-data-are-considered-together)).

<details class="model-construction-details">
<summary><strong>Expand to read about feature preprocessing</strong></summary>

<div class="model-details-box">

Before entering the Gaussian elastic-net regression, predictors were processed by modality:

- **Expression and copy number:** missing values were replaced with the training-set median. Each feature was then centred and standardized:

  \[
  z = \frac{x - \text{training mean}}{\text{training SD}}
  \]
- **Damaging mutations:** missing values were replaced with the most common training-set category, encoded as 0/1, and then centred and standardized using the training-set mutation prevalence and SD.
- **Cancer lineage:** represented by 0/1 indicator variables relative to the most common lineage. These indicators were not standardized and were the only unpenalized predictors.
- **Chronos dependency:** used as the continuous outcome on its original scale rather than standardized, so predictions, residuals and RMSE remain directly interpretable in Chronos units.

For nested cross-validation, imputation values, means and SDs were calculated using only the corresponding outer training set and then applied unchanged to its held-out cell lines. The final full-data model calculated a new set of preprocessing values from the complete dataset.

All molecular features—including target characterisation, pre-specified hypotheses and remaining genome-wide features—received the same modality-appropriate preprocessing and the same penalty factor. `glmnet` was run with `standardize = FALSE` because standardization had already been performed explicitly.

</div>

</details>

```{r integrated-model-text, results='asis'}
stable.predictors <- selection.stability[selection.stability$stable, ]
if (nrow(stable.predictors)) {
  cat(sprintf(
    "The integrated procedure identified **%d stable molecular predictor%s**. These are exploratory predictors associated with `%s` dependency.\n",
    nrow(stable.predictors), ifelse(nrow(stable.predictors) == 1L, "", "s"), target
  ))
} else {
  cat(sprintf(
    "After fitting this model, no molecular feature met all stability criteria for `%s`. This is a valid result: the full-data model was fitted with every eligible molecular feature, but none was reproducible enough to enter the reported stable set.\n",
    target
  ))
}
```

```{r molecular-model-summary}
modality.labels <- c(
  expression = "Expression",
  mutation = "Damaging mutation",
  copy_number = "Copy number"
)
source.labels <- c(
  target_characterization = "Target characterisation",
  prespecified_hypothesis = "Pre-specified hypothesis",
  genome_wide_candidate = "Genome-wide candidate"
)
molecular.model.summary <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  names(source.labels),
  function(source.name) do.call(rbind, lapply(
    names(modality.labels),
    function(modality.name) {
      molecular.results <- selection.stability[
        selection.stability$role == source.name &
          selection.stability$modality == modality.name,
      ]
      if (!nrow(molecular.results)) return(NULL)
      data.frame(
        Source = source.labels[[source.name]],
        Modality = modality.labels[[modality.name]],
        `Eligible predictors entered` = nrow(molecular.results),
        `Selected in at least one outer model` = sum(
          molecular.results$selected_count > 0
        ),
        `Stable predictors` = sum(molecular.results$stable),
        check.names = FALSE
      )
    }
  ))
))
knitr::kable(
  molecular.model.summary,
  caption = "Integrated molecular-search results by source and modality"
)
```

```{r hypothesis-fate-table}
  Status = ifelse(
```

```{r stable-predictor-interpretation, results='asis'}
if (nrow(stable.predictors)) {
  for (predictor.index in seq_len(nrow(stable.predictors))) {
    predictor <- stable.predictors[predictor.index, ]
    feature.phrase <- if (predictor$modality == "mutation") {
      paste("the presence of", predictor$label)
    } else {
      paste("higher", predictor$label)
    }
    dependency.direction <- if (predictor$full_discovery_coefficient < 0) {
      paste("stronger", target, "dependency")
    } else {
      paste("weaker", target, "dependency")
    }
    cat(sprintf(
      "**%s** was kept in **%d of %d** repeated model fits. In **%.0f%%** of those fits, %s pointed toward **%s**. In the full-data model, a one-SD increase changed the predicted Chronos score by **%s**.\n\n",
      predictor$label,
      predictor$selected_count,
      predictor$models_evaluated,
      100 * predictor$direction_concordance,
      feature.phrase,
      dependency.direction,
      format_report_number(predictor$full_discovery_coefficient)
    ))
    if (abs(predictor$selection_frequency - 0.60) < 1e-12) {
      cat("This is exactly the minimum selection frequency required for the stable label, so the result is borderline stable rather than highly consistent.\n\n")
    }
  }
}
```

# Performance on held-out cell lines

The model was tested on cell lines that were not used to train it. This estimates how well its predictions may generalise to new data.

```{r model-performance-text, results='asis'}
rmse.mean <- mean(model.performance$rmse)
rmse.sd <- sd(model.performance$rmse)
pearson.mean <- mean(model.performance$pearson_r)
pearson.sd <- sd(model.performance$pearson_r)
r2.mean <- mean(model.performance$r_squared)
r2.sd <- sd(model.performance$r_squared)
dependency.sd <- dependency$sd[1]
rmse.relative <- rmse.mean / dependency.sd
pearson.range <- range(model.performance$pearson_r)
r2.range <- range(model.performance$r_squared)
rmse.range <- range(model.performance$rmse)
pearson.consistency <- if (diff(pearson.range) <= 0.05) {
  "similar across repeats"
} else {
  "varied across repeats"
}
r2.consistency <- if (diff(r2.range) <= 0.05) {
  "similar across repeats"
} else {
  "varied across repeats"
}
rmse.consistency <- if (diff(rmse.range) <= 0.05 * dependency.sd) {
  "similar across repeats"
} else {
  "varied across repeats"
}

cat(sprintf(
  "**Pearson r** compares the pattern of predicted and observed values. It asks whether cell lines predicted to have high dependency scores actually have high observed scores, and whether those predicted to have low scores actually have low observed scores. The mean held-out Pearson r was **%s** (range %s to %s), showing how closely the model ranked observed dependency scores. The Pearson r results were **%s**.\n\n",
  format_report_number(pearson.mean),
  format_report_number(pearson.range[1]),
  format_report_number(pearson.range[2]),
  pearson.consistency
))

r2.result.description <- if (r2.mean < 0) {
  sprintf(
    "On average, the model performed worse than assigning every cell line the average observed `%s` dependency score.",
    target
  )
} else if (r2.mean == 0) {
  sprintf(
    "On average, the model performed the same as assigning every cell line the average observed `%s` dependency score.",
    target
  )
} else {
  sprintf(
    "On average, the model reduced the total squared prediction error by approximately **%.1f%%** relative to assigning every cell line the average observed `%s` dependency score.",
    100 * r2.mean, target
  )
}
cat(sprintf(
  "**R-squared** measures numerical prediction accuracy by comparing the model's total squared prediction errors with those from assigning every cell line the average observed dependency score. An R-squared of 1 represents perfect predictions, 0 means the model is no better than that average-only reference, and a negative value means it is worse. The mean held-out R-squared was **%s** (range %s to %s). %s The R-squared results were **%s**.\n\n",
  format_report_number(r2.mean),
  format_report_number(r2.range[1]),
  format_report_number(r2.range[2]),
  r2.result.description,
  r2.consistency
))

cat(sprintf(
  "**RMSE** summarises the typical size of the difference between predicted and observed dependency scores, with larger errors receiving more weight. The mean held-out RMSE was **%s Chronos units** (range %s to %s), equivalent to **%.1f%%** of the observed `%s` dependency SD of %s. Lower values indicate predictions closer to the observed scores, and 0 represents perfect predictions. The RMSE results were **%s**.\n\n",
  format_report_number(rmse.mean),
  format_report_number(rmse.range[1]),
  format_report_number(rmse.range[2]),
  100 * rmse.relative,
  target,
  format_report_number(dependency.sd),
  rmse.consistency
))

performance.description <- if (r2.mean <= 0) {
  "no useful"
} else if (r2.mean < 0.10) {
  "limited"
} else if (r2.mean < 0.30) {
  "modest"
} else if (r2.mean < 0.50) {
  "moderate"
} else {
  "strong"
}
cat(sprintf(
  "Based on R-squared, the model therefore had **%s held-out predictive performance**.\n\n",
  performance.description
))
cat("This performance describes the complete model, including cancer lineage and all molecular features selected within each training fold. It cannot be attributed to any single retained gene.\n")
```

For exploratory feature prioritisation, a positive and consistent held-out R-squared indicates useful signal. Accurate prediction of individual cell lines would require substantially smaller errors and independent validation.

## Observed versus predicted dependency

The three panels show the three complete cross-validation repeats. Every point is a cell line predicted while it was held out from model fitting and feature selection. The dashed diagonal marks a perfect prediction, where the predicted score equals the observed score. The vertical distance between a point and this line is the prediction error for that cell line: larger distances increase RMSE and reduce R-squared.

```{r observed-predicted-figure, out.width='100%', fig.align='center'}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figure.dir, "08_observed_vs_predicted.png"))
```

## Performance by lineage

This comparison asks whether the model predicts differences among cell lines *within* each cancer lineage. A lineage R-squared above zero means the model improves on assigning every cell line that lineage's average dependency score; a negative value means it performs worse than that simple reference. Only lineages with at least 10 models are shown. Lineage estimates are less precise than the pan-cancer result and should be treated as diagnostic rather than as separate validated models.

```{r lineage-performance-text, results='asis'}
positive.lineage.count <- sum(lineage.performance$r_squared_mean > 0)
modest.lineage.count <- sum(lineage.performance$r_squared_mean >= 0.10)
best.lineage <- lineage.performance[
  which.max(lineage.performance$r_squared_mean),
]
worst.lineage <- lineage.performance[
  which.min(lineage.performance$r_squared_mean),
]
cat(sprintf(
  "The model had positive held-out R-squared in **%d of %d lineages**, and **%d lineages reached R-squared 0.10**. The highest value was observed in **%s** (R-squared %s; RMSE %s), while the lowest was observed in **%s** (R-squared %s; RMSE %s).",
  positive.lineage.count,
  nrow(lineage.performance),
  modest.lineage.count,
  best.lineage$lineage,
  format_report_number(best.lineage$r_squared_mean),
  format_report_number(best.lineage$rmse_mean),
  worst.lineage$lineage,
  format_report_number(worst.lineage$r_squared_mean),
  format_report_number(worst.lineage$rmse_mean)
))
if (modest.lineage.count == 0L) {
  if (r2.mean > 0) {
    cat(sprintf(
      "\n\nFor `%s`, the positive pan-cancer R-squared therefore should not be interpreted as evidence that the model can reliably rank cell lines within individual cancer types. The pattern suggests that much of the overall predictive performance comes from differences between lineages.",
      target
    ))
  } else {
    cat(sprintf(
      "\n\nFor `%s`, this is consistent with the lack of useful predictive performance in the pan-cancer analysis: the model did not reliably rank cell lines either overall or within individual cancer types.",
      target
    ))
  }
}
```

```{r lineage-performance-figure, out.width='90%', fig.align='center'}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figure.dir, "09_lineage_cv_performance.png"))
```

```{r model-performance-table}
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(
  model.performance.display,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Nested-cross-validation performance by repeat"
)
```

</details>

# Conclusion, interpretation and limitations

This report asked which molecular features are associated with dependency on **`r target`** and whether exploratory molecular predictors recur when all eligible modalities are considered jointly. It first described dependency and lineage patterns, retained the pan-cancer univariate screens as descriptive analyses, and followed eligible target/pre-specified-hypothesis associations within individual lineages. The integrated model then allowed every eligible molecular feature to compete under the same elastic-net penalty while accounting for different lineage baselines. It estimates common molecular effects; formal lineage-dependent molecular effects would require a separate feature-by-lineage interaction analysis.

The resulting stable genes, when present, are exploratory molecular predictors rather than causal genes or independently significant effects. Their evidence is summarized by repeated outer-fold selection frequency, coefficient-direction concordance, persistence in the full-data fit and nested-CV performance.

Specifically:


```{r conclusion-results, results='asis'}
cat(sprintf(
  "Across **%d pancancer models**, the median `%s` Chronos score was **%s**, and **%.1f%%** of models had a score below -0.5. ",
  dependency$n,
  target,
  format_report_number(dependency$median),
  100 * dependency$proportion_below_minus_0_5
))

conclusion.lineages <- lineages[
  !is.na(lineages$fdr) &
    lineages$fdr < 0.05 &
    lineages$median_difference < 0,
]

if (!is.na(lineage.global$p_value) && lineage.global$p_value < 0.05) {
  if (nrow(conclusion.lineages)) {
    conclusion.lineages <- conclusion.lineages[
      order(conclusion.lineages$fdr, conclusion.lineages$median_difference),
    ]
    conclusion.lineage.names <- head(conclusion.lineages$lineage, 2L)
    cat(sprintf(
      "Dependency varied across cancer lineages, with **%s** among the contexts showing a stronger dependency than models from remaining lineages. ",
      paste(conclusion.lineage.names, collapse = "** and **")
    ))
  } else {
    cat("Dependency varied across cancer lineages, although no individual stronger-dependency lineage passed the 5% FDR threshold. ")
  }
} else {
  cat("There was no clear evidence that dependency varied across cancer lineages. ")
}

if (nrow(stable.predictors)) {
  stable.names <- paste0(
    "**", stable.predictors$gene, " ",
    gsub("_", " ", stable.predictors$modality), "**"
  )
  cat(sprintf(
    "\n\nThe stable molecular predictor set contained %s. These findings require independent biological validation.\n",
    paste(stable.names, collapse = ", ")
  ))
} else {
  cat(sprintf(
    "\n\nNo molecular feature satisfied the stability criteria for `%s`; no predictor was added merely to make the reported stable set non-empty.\n",
    target
  ))
}
```

These results provide a prioritisation map for validation in independent, lineage-balanced models. Copy number predictors should also be tested to determine whether they represent the named gene or a broader chromosomal event. A useful next experiment is to ask whether a stable or near-miss predictor reproducibly separates models with stronger and weaker `r target` dependency under an independent genetic or pharmacological perturbation.

The inverse question: *which dependencies are selective in models carrying mutation of a chosen tumour suppressor?* requires a different feature-centric genome-wide dependency screen and remains outside this repository's current scope. However, a good starting point is [Haider *et al.*, Nature Genetics 57, 522–529 (2025)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-025-02108-2), and its associated [SYLVER app](https://software.icr.ac.uk/app/sylver/) for exploring selective dependencies in the context of specific mutations.
Stay in touch with the repository for future developments.

# Reproducibility

The pipeline saves summary tables, figures and the completed report locally. Raw DepMap matrices and cell-line-level intermediate files remain excluded from version control; users must obtain the source data from DepMap (see README) and regenerate the intermediate files by running the pipeline to obtain a copy of this report with a new target gene.
